claims.claim: The Sabbath law is re-issued (Ex 35:1–3, cf. Ex 31:12–17) before any work on the tabernacle begins, with the added ban on kindling fire on the Sabbath.
claims.evidence: Ex 35:1–3 (KJV, read in full); K&D Ex 35

claims.claim: The Sabbath command stands first so that even the sacred work of building the tabernacle is bounded by it.
claims.evidence: Ex 35:1–3; K&D Ex 35: the no-fire rule "was to be observed even in connection with the work to be done for the tabernacle"

claims.claim: Sabbath work carries the death penalty (Ex 35:2), and the Sabbath is "a sabbath of rest" (*šabbat šabbātôn*).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:2; BDB H7676 sense 1d (*šabbat šabbātôn*, Ex 35:2)

claims.claim: The offerings for the tabernacle are freewill only — "whosoever is of a willing heart" (Ex 35:5).
The materials list of Ex 35:5–9 repeats the list of Ex 25:3–7.
The people offered their personal gold jewellery — bracelets, earrings, rings, tablets (Ex 35:22).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:22; K&D Ex 35 on the terms (*ḥāḥ, nezem, tabbaʿat, kûmāz*)

claims.claim: The gold and silver for the tabernacle came from the Egyptian spoil (Ex 12:35–36), Amalekite spoil, and trade with neighbouring peoples.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 38:25; K&D Ex 38 (Egyptian gold mines; Arab caravan trade)

claims.claim: The women spun the yarn (blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen) and the goats' hair with their hands (Ex 35:25–26).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:25–26; K&D Ex 35 (the cloth was dyed in the yarn, as in Egypt)

claims.claim: The rulers (princes) brought the onyx stones and the spices for the anointing oil and incense (Ex 35:27–28).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:27–28; K&D Ex 35 ("who had such costly things in their possession")

claims.claim: The offering is termed *tĕrûmâ* (heave-offering, Ex 35:24) and the gold a *tĕnûpâ* (wave-offering, Ex 35:22; 38:24); the two terms overlap in this context.
claims.evidence: Ex 35:22, 24; 38:24, 29; K&D Ex 35 (tenuphah/terumah discussion)

claims.claim: The whole congregation's giving is summed as a "willing offering" (Ex 35:29).
The re-issue of the Sabbath here is the literary hinge between the covenant's renewal (Ex 34) and the building (Ex 35–40).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 35 ("After the restoration of the covenant..."); Childs, second-hand via *Perspective Digest* (Ex 32–34 as the theological hinge)

claims.claim: Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, is called by name (Ex 35:30).
Bezalel's name means "in the shadow (protection) of El".
claims.evidence: BDB H1212

claims.claim: Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all workmanship (Ex 35:31); *ḥoḵmâ* here denotes technical skill.
claims.evidence: Ex 35:31; BDB H2451 sense 1 (skill in technical work, Ex 35:26, 31, 35; 36:1–2)

claims.claim: Aholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, is named as Bezalel's fellow (Ex 35:34); his name means "Father's tent".
claims.evidence: Ex 35:34; BDB H171

claims.claim: The pairing of Judah and Dan — the leading tribe and a lowly tribe — shows the work joining the whole people.
claims.evidence: The tribal pairing is in the text (Ex 35:30, 34); the reading is a traditional observation, not stated in the text

claims.claim: Bezalel is given the ability to teach, that is, to instruct labourers under his supervision (Ex 35:34).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:34; K&D Ex 35 ("had qualified him to instruct labourers to prepare the different articles under his supervision")

claims.claim: The "wise-hearted" (*ḥăḵam-lēb*) are summoned to make all that the LORD commanded (Ex 35:10; 36:1–2).
claims.evidence: Ex 35:10; 36:1–2; Calvin on Ex 35:10 ("the artificers, who excelled in shrewdness of intellect")

claims.claim: Moses hands the people's offerings to the craftsmen, and the people keep bringing freewill offerings every morning (Ex 36:3).
The craftsmen report the surplus — "The people bring much more than enough" (Ex 36:5).
Moses proclaims a restraint through the camp: no man or woman is to make any more work for the offering of the sanctuary (Ex 36:6).
claims.evidence: Ex 36:6; K&D Ex 36 (*mĕlā'khāh* = property)

claims.claim: "The stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much" (Ex 36:7); the liberal contribution proved the people's willingness to uphold the covenant.
claims.evidence: Ex 36:7; K&D Ex 36 (the willingness reading)

claims.claim: Ex 38:22–23 names Bezalel and Aholiab as the makers of all that the LORD commanded Moses, with Aholiab described as engraver, cunning workman, and embroiderer.
Ex 36–39 repeats the instructions of Ex 25–31 nearly verbatim.
claims.evidence: The text as read; K&D cross-refers each execution section to chs. 25–30

claims.claim: The repetition's purpose is to show the exact conformity of the execution to the command.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 38:1 ("in which may be traced the exact conformity of the execution to the order"); Clarke Ex 39:32

claims.claim: The refrain "as the LORD commanded Moses" (exact and variant forms) recurs through Ex 39 and Ex 40.
The ten linen curtains (28 × 4 cubits, cherubim, 50 gold clasps) and the eleven goats'-hair curtains (30 × 4 cubits, 50 bronze clasps) are made (Ex 36:8–18).
The coverings are rams' skins dyed red and *taḥaš* skins (Ex 36:19).
claims.evidence: Ex 36:19; cf. Ex 26:14 (identity of *taḥaš*: clm-bu-030)

claims.claim: The identity of *taḥaš* (KJV "badgers' skins") is uncertain: BDB suggests probably the dugong, with sheep-skin and Egyptian leather as alternatives; JFB suggests the dugong or dolphin of the Red Sea; the LXX renders it "blue skins".
claims.evidence: BDB H8476; JFB Ex 39:34; NETS Ex 36:19

claims.claim: The 48 boards of acacia (*šittîm*) wood are 10 × 1.5 cubits, two tenons each, with silver sockets, gold overlay, five bars and a middle bar (Ex 36:20–34).
The veil hangs on four gold-overlaid pillars with silver sockets; the door hanging on five pillars with bronze sockets (Ex 36:35–38).

Bezalel personally makes the ark, 2.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 cubits, overlaid with gold within and without, with the mercy seat and two cherubim (Ex 37:1–9); the ark, as the most holy thing, is expressly his work.
claims.evidence: Ex 37:1–9; K&D Ex 37 ("as being the most holy thing of all, is distinguished above all the rest, by being expressly mentioned as the work of Bezaleel, the chief architect")

claims.claim: The table, the lampstand (one talent of pure gold, seven lamps), the incense altar, the anointing oil and the incense are made (Ex 37:10–29).
claims.evidence: Ex 37:10–29, esp. 37:24 ("Of a talent of pure gold made he it, and all the vessels thereof")

claims.claim: The burnt-offering altar is 5 × 5 × 3 cubits, of bronze, hollow with boards (Ex 38:1–7).
The laver is made of bronze from the mirrors (*marʾôt*) of the women assembling at the door of the tabernacle (Ex 38:8).
claims.evidence: Ex 38:8; Clarke Ex 38 (*marʾôt* from *raah*, "he saw"; mirrors of polished metal, glass not yet in use); JFB Ex 38:8 ("The word mirrors should have been used")

claims.claim: The women at the door were women of pious character who frequented the courts, not priestesses; their surrender of their mirrors was a renunciation like the Nazarite's hair.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 38:8 (Hengstenberg); Clarke Ex 38 (*tsābāʾ* = troops keeping watch; cf. 1 Sam 2:22)

claims.claim: The court is 100 × 50 cubits, with 20 + 20 + 10 + 10 pillars, bronze sockets, silver hooks and bands (Ex 38:9–20).
claims.evidence: Ex 38:9–20; cf. Ex 27:9–19; JFB Ex 38:9 (150 ft × 75 ft, curtains about eight feet high)

claims.claim: The priestly garments are made (Ex 39:1–31): ephod with onyx shoulder stones, breastplate with twelve stones in four rows of three, robe of blue with pomegranates and gold bells, linen coats, mitre, bonnets, breeches, girdle, and the gold plate "HOLINESS TO THE LORD".
The Urim and Thummim are not mentioned in Ex 39 (cf. Ex 28:30).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 39 ("The Urim and Thummim are not mentioned")

claims.claim: The gold plate's inscription follows the Egyptian practice of seal-rings bearing the owner's name and a religious sentiment.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 39:30

claims.claim: The accounting (Ex 38:21–31) was made by the Levites under Ithamar son of Aaron, by Moses' command; *pĕqûdîm* is a reckoning of weight and worth.
claims.evidence: Ex 38:21; K&D Ex 38

claims.claim: Gold 29 talents 730 shekels; silver 100 talents 1,775 shekels from 603,550 men at a half-shekel (bekah) each; bronze 70 talents 2,400 shekels (Ex 38:24–29).
The silver total implies the census of 603,550 men aged twenty and upward, and proves a talent contained 3,000 shekels (603,550 × ½ = 301,775 = 100 talents + 1,775 shekels).
claims.evidence: Ex 38:25–26; K&D Ex 38 ("which proves by the way that a talent contained 3000 shekels")

claims.claim: The 100 talents of silver were cast into 100 sockets — 96 for the 48 boards and 4 for the veil pillars — one talent per socket; the 1,775 shekels made the hooks, the silvering of the capitals, and the connecting rods (Ex 38:27–28).
The freewill silver offerings (Ex 35:24) are not included in the Ex 38:25 total, which counts only the atonement money (Ex 30:12).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 38

claims.claim: The quantities of gold and silver are modest beside the treasures of the ancient East, and the materials came from Egyptian spoil and Arab caravan trade; the gold amounts to 87,730 shekels (K&D's text prints "87,370", an evident misprint, as its own figure of 877,300 thalers shows).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 38 (Belus temple; Sardanapalus; Cyrus; Alexander at Susa and Persepolis; Egyptian gold mines; Arab caravan trade; Thenius's estimate, 10 thalers per gold shekel = 877,300 thalers, £131,595)

claims.claim: "Thus was all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of the congregation finished" (Ex 39:32).
The finished work is brought to Moses (Ex 39:33–41); "the tent" in 39:33 is the two tent-cloths, the variegated cloth forming the inner walls.
Moses inspects the work, finds it done as the LORD commanded, and blesses the people (Ex 39:43).
claims.evidence: Ex 39:43; JFB Ex 39:43 ("A formal inspection... to ascertain whether it corresponded with 'the pattern'"); Clarke Ex 39:43 (Moses as general superintendent; the blessing pronounced upon all)

claims.claim: The erection is commanded for the first day of the first month of the second year (Ex 40:2, 17); the building took about six months.
claims.evidence: Ex 40:2, 17; Clarke Ex 40:2; K&D Ex 40 ("not quite half a year"); JFB Ex 40:2

claims.claim: The erection order is: sockets, boards, bars, pillars; tent spread over; ark placed with the testimony inside; veil hung; table (north), lampstand (south), incense altar (before the veil); burnt-offering altar; laver; court (Ex 40:17–33).
"The testimony" placed in the ark is the decalogue on the two tables of stone (Ex 31:18; 25:16), not "the revelation, so far as it existed already".
claims.evidence: Ex 40:20; K&D Ex 40 (against Knobel)

claims.claim: The anointing of the tabernacle and vessels commanded in Ex 40:9–11 did not take place at the erection but at the consecration of Aaron (Lev 8:10–11).
The vessels were holy by being built according to God's instructions and by the glory's filling, not first by the anointing, which sanctified them for the nation's use.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 40

claims.claim: "So Moses finished the work" (Ex 40:33) echoes Gen 2:2, where God finishes his work; the book's ending mirrors creation's completion.
claims.evidence: Ex 40:33; Gen 2:2 (the verbal parallel *wayĕkhal*; widely noted — see §8)

claims.claim: The cloud covered the tent and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex 40:34).
The glory filling the dwelling is distinguished from the cloud coming down upon the tabernacle: the cloud covers, the glory fills.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 40 ("the glory of Jehovah filling the dwelling is clearly distinguished from the cloud coming down upon the tabernacle")

claims.claim: Moses was unable to enter because the cloud abode and the glory filled the tabernacle (Ex 40:35); the same happened at Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 8:10–11).
claims.evidence: Ex 40:35; 1 Kgs 8:10–11; Clarke Ex 40:34; K&D Ex 40

claims.claim: The cloud afterwards withdrew into the most holy place, above the outspread wings of the cherubim, so that Moses and the priests could enter the holy place.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 40 (inference; the text does not state the withdrawal)

claims.claim: The cloud and the fire guided all the journeys: rising = travel, resting = encamp (Ex 40:36–38), elaborated in Num 9:15–23.
The completed tabernacle is erected on New Year's Day, underscoring that a new era in the life of the people has begun.
claims.evidence: Sarna, second-hand (p. 156, via the *Good Word* 2025 Q3 guide)

claims.claim: The tabernacle's function is to create "a portable Sinai, a means by which a continued avenue of communication with God could be maintained".
claims.evidence: Sarna, second-hand (p. 237, via Reform Judaism / My Jewish Learning / Rabbinical Assembly)

claims.claim: The presence of God which once abode on Mount Sinai now dwells in the sanctuary and accompanies Israel; the tabernacle's role in ch. 40 is to extend the Sinai experience by a permanent cultic institution.
claims.evidence: Childs, second-hand (p. 638, via the Pekudei parasha; the "extend the Sinai experience" formulation via *Perspective Digest*)

claims.claim: The tabernacle is a portable, movable sanctuary — "a movable and ambulatory temple" — carried on poles, not a fixed building.
Portable sanctuaries of this kind existed in the Late Bronze Age world: Ramesses II's war tent at Kadesh is the most striking parallel.
claims.evidence: Homan (2002), second-hand via the mcgilvaryhouse Exodus page

claims.claim: At Timna, Rothenberg excavated a small Egyptian Hathor shrine (Seti I, late 13th c. BCE) that Midianites in the 12th c. BCE turned into a tent sanctuary with dyed linen and wool, post-holes, and a gilt-headed copper serpent in the innermost chamber.
claims.evidence: Secondary accounts read: madainproject ("Shrine of Hathor (Timna)"); livingpassages ("The Bronze Serpent and the Pole"); corroborated by the BibleHub Q&A on Ex 38:10. The primary excavation report was not read.

claims.claim: The Midianite connection matters because Moses' in-laws were Midianites (Ex 2:15–21; 18:1), so Israel's tent-shrine tradition may have drawn on Midianite practice.
claims.evidence: The kinship is Established (Ex 2:15–21; 18:1); the inference of influence has no direct evidence

claims.claim: The *tabnît* is a "pattern, according to which anything is to be constructed" — of the tabernacle (Ex 25:9, 40), of the temple (1 Chr 28:11), and of the altar (2 Kgs 16:10).
claims.evidence: BDB H8403 sense 2

claims.claim: Philo reads the tabernacle as a copy of the world: the four materials are the four elements (flax = earth, purple = water, hyacinth = air, scarlet = fire); the candlestick's seven lamps are the seven planets; the twelve breastplate stones are the zodiac.
claims.evidence: Philo, Vit. Mos. II §§84–88, 101–103, 117–135 (read in full)

claims.claim: Josephus's cosmic reading derives from Philo.
claims.evidence: Whiston's footnote to Ant. 3.7.7 ("this explication... is taken out of Philo"), read via Perseus

claims.claim: Josephus divides the tabernacle into three parts corresponding to land, sea, and heaven, the third set apart for God alone.
claims.evidence: Josephus, Ant. 3.7.7 (read in full via Perseus)

claims.claim: The text gives a relative date: the erection on the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus (Ex 40:17).
The absolute date is debated: the early date (15th c., traditional 1446 BCE) against the late date (13th c., Ramesses II).
claims.evidence: See §7; the positions are well established, the choice is not

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the earliest extra-biblical reference to Israel; it sets a *terminus ante quem* — Israel was a people in Canaan by 1208 BCE.
claims.evidence: Merneptah Stele, verified via the Biblical Archaeology article, read in full (line 27; the people determinative; Petrie 1896; Spiegelberg; JE 31408); Egyptian Museum, Cairo, JE 31408.

claims.claim: The stele does not settle the exodus date: both the early and the late dates precede 1208 BCE.
claims.evidence: §7 reasoning; the late date leaves little room for forty years plus conquest and settlement, which is an argument, not a proof

claims.claim: The LXX reorders the construction account: the garments (MT Ex 39) come first within LXX Ex 36, then the curtains/boards (MT 36) as LXX 37, the furniture (MT 37) as LXX 38, the altar/court/amounts (MT 38) as LXX 39, and the erection (MT 40) as LXX 40.
claims.evidence: NETS Exodus (Perkins), read in full for Ex 35–40

claims.claim: The LXX renders *taḥaš* as "blue skins" and *ʾohŏlîʾāb* as "Eliab".
The LXX renders the bekah as "one drachma" (LXX 39:26); cf. Clarke on the LXX's rendering of the shekel as *didrachmon*.
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 39:2 (LXX numbering); Clarke Ex 38

claims.claim: The LXX says the bronze altar was made "from the bronze fire-pans that belonged to the men who revolted with the gathering of Kore" (LXX 38:22) — a plus harmonizing with Num 16:36–39.
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 38:22 (as a fact about the LXX text; the historical claim is a harmonization)

claims.claim: The LXX renders the women at the door as "the women who fasted, who fasted by the doors of the tent of witness" (LXX 38:26).
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 38:26 (as a fact about the LXX text)

claims.claim: It is not clear whether the same person translated Ex 1–34 and Ex 35–40.
claims.evidence: NETS, "To the Reader of Exodus"

claims.claim: Jubilees 1 places the giving of the law in the first year of the exodus, the third month, the 16th day, 2450 A.M., with Moses on the mount forty days and forty nights and the promise "until I descend and dwell with them throughout eternity".
claims.evidence: Jubilees ch. 1 (Charles; read in full)

claims.claim: Augustine (Civ. Dei XVI.43) places the tabernacle's dedication after the law given on the fiftieth day after Passover, and reads the Passover as a type of Christ and Moses' not entering the land as prefiguring Joshua/Jesus.
claims.evidence: Augustine, Civ. Dei XVI.43 (Dods; read in full)

claims.claim: The New Testament reads the tabernacle as a copy and shadow of the heavenly (Heb 8:5; 9:23–24) and as fulfilled in the Word who "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14).
claims.evidence: Heb 8:5; 9:23–24; John 1:14 (the typological reading itself is Traditional; see §8)

claims.claim: Exodus ends not with a law or a march but with God's presence dwelling among Israel — the glory filling the tabernacle is the book's climax.
claims.evidence: The literary shape of Ex 40:34–38 as the book's close; Childs/Sarna, second-hand (§2.2)

date.note: The date of the Exodus is debated (early vs. late); pending research question R1. The alternative, a proposed early date of 1446 BCE, is a material decision not being made now. Chronology is narrative only.
